title: CUET Political Science Test 14
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Congress (R)'s tally in the 1971 Lok Sabha election
questions.question: In the 1971 Lok Sabha election, the Congress (R) and its allies won ________ seats.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 352
Why: The Congress (R)-CPI alliance won 375 seats, of which the Congress (R) won 352.
Why not the others:
(A) 283 was the Congress tally of 1967.
(C) and (D) are close to the Congress tally of 1984.
Key point: The 1971 result restored the Congress to dominance.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Wars and treaties, 1962–1972, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Simla Agreement is signed
(B) China and India go to war
(C) The Tashkent Agreement is signed
(D) India and the USSR sign a Treaty of Peace and Friendship
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C), (D), (A)
Why: (B) The war with China came in 1962. (C) The Tashkent Agreement followed in 1966. (D) The Indo-Soviet treaty was signed in 1971. (A) The Simla Agreement came in 1972.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Indo-Soviet treaty before Tashkent. Option (B) puts Tashkent before the war with China. Option (C) puts Simla before the Indo-Soviet treaty.
Key point: 1962 → 1966 → 1971 → 1972.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Not among the issues in the politics of the North-East
questions.question: Which of the following has NOT been a major issue in the politics of the North-East?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Demands to join Pakistan
Why: The North-East's politics has centred on autonomy, secession and opposition to outsiders. Joining Pakistan has not been an issue.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are the three issues NCERT names.
Key point: Three issues dominate the politics of the North-East.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Article used to dismiss the Kerala government in 1959
questions.question: The Communist government of Kerala was dismissed in 1959 under Article ________ of the Constitution.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 356
Why: The Centre used Article 356 to dismiss the Kerala government in 1959.
Why not the others:
(B) Article 352 deals with a national emergency.
(C) Article 370 concerned Jammu and Kashmir.
(D) Article 368 deals with amending the Constitution.
Key point: The 1959 dismissal was a controversial use of Article 356.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: The Emergency and the 1977 election — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975.
(B) It was proclaimed on the ground of a threat of internal disturbance.
(C) Lok Sabha elections were held in March 1977.
(D) The Janata Party won a majority of the seats in every State in 1977.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: the Congress did very well in the southern States in 1977.
Why not the others: Option (B) leaves out the true statement (B). Options (C) and (D) include the false statement (D).
Key point: The Janata wave of 1977 was strongest in the north.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Reason behind India's non-aligned stance
questions.question: What was the main purpose of India's policy of non-alignment?
options: A) To join the Soviet bloc in secret
B) To keep out of both Cold War blocs
C) To obey a UN rule that new states stay neutral
D) To make up for having no armed forces
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To keep out of both Cold War blocs
Why: Non-alignment let India keep away from both military blocs and judge each issue on its merits.
Why not the others:
(A) India did not join either bloc.
(C) The UN made no such demand.
(D) India had its own armed forces.
Key point: Non-alignment meant independence in foreign policy, not isolation.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Why 'non-Congressism' arose
questions.question: Why did leaders like Ram Manohar Lohia call for 'non-Congressism' in the 1960s?
options: A) Because they wanted to merge all their parties into the Congress
B) Because they believed elections should be suspended for some years
C) Because the Congress had refused to contest any election after 1962
D) Because they saw Congress dominance as undemocratic and harmful to the poor
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because they saw Congress dominance as undemocratic and harmful to the poor
Why: Lohia argued that Congress rule was undemocratic and against the interests of ordinary people, so opposition parties should unite against it.
Why not the others:
(A) They wanted to defeat the Congress, not join it.
(B) They wanted to win elections, not stop them.
(C) The Congress contested every election.
Key point: Non-Congressism brought ideologically different parties together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Institution at the centre of the Soviet system
questions.question: The political system of the Soviet Union revolved around the ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Communist Party
Why: The Communist Party dominated every part of the Soviet system.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were all under the party's control.
Key point: The USSR was a one-party state.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Not a challenge of nation-building after 1947
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the challenges independent India faced in building the nation?
options: A) Building an overseas colonial empire
B) Shaping a nation that was united yet diverse
D) Ensuring the development and well-being of all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Building an overseas colonial empire
Why: India faced the challenges of unity, democracy and development. Building an empire was never one of them.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are the three challenges NCERT names.
Key point: Unity, democracy and development were the three challenges.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Soviet state and party — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Soviet economy was based on state ownership.
(B) Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Union in 1975.
(C) The Communist Party controlled all the institutions of the state.
(D) The CIS was formed in December 1991.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: Gorbachev became General Secretary in 1985.
Why not the others: (A) The economy was state-owned. (C) The party dominated all institutions. (D) The CIS came in December 1991. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Gorbachev's reforms began in 1985.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Dimensions of globalisation
questions.question:
Match List-I (Dimension) with List-II (Example).

List-I
(A) Economic
(B) Cultural
(C) Political
(D) Technological

List-II
(I) Spread of foreign food and dress habits
(II) Erosion of the capacity of states
(III) Growth of the internet and mobile phones
(IV) Greater flows of trade and capital
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Economic globalisation means more trade and capital flows (IV). Cultural globalisation spreads foreign food and dress (I). Politically, it can erode state capacity (II). Technology such as the internet drives it (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps economic and cultural. Option (B) swaps cultural and political. Option (C) swaps political and technological.
Key point: Globalisation has economic, political, cultural and technological dimensions.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Coalitions and the parties that led them
questions.question:
Match List-I (Coalition) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) NDA
(B) UPA
(C) United Front
(D) National Front

List-II
(I) Coalition of 1996 in which the Janata Dal was the leading party
(II) Coalition that formed the government under V.P. Singh in 1989
(III) Coalition led by the Congress from 2004
(IV) Coalition led by the BJP
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The NDA is led by the BJP (IV). The UPA was led by the Congress (III). The United Front of 1996 was led by the Janata Dal (I). The National Front formed the 1989 government (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the NDA and UPA. Option (B) swaps the UPA and United Front. Option (D) swaps the United Front and National Front.
Key point: Coalitions have formed around both national parties and third forces.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Steps towards the UN, 1941–1945, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Declaration by United Nations is signed
(B) The UN Charter is signed at San Francisco
(C) The Atlantic Charter is signed
(D) The Yalta Conference is held
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: (C) The Atlantic Charter came in August 1941. (A) The Declaration by United Nations came in January 1942. (D) The Yalta Conference met in February 1945. (B) The Charter was signed in June 1945.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Declaration before the Atlantic Charter. Option (B) puts the Charter before Yalta. Option (D) puts Yalta before the Declaration.
Key point: 1941 → 1942 → February 1945 → June 1945.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: River at the centre of the Farakka dispute
questions.question: India and Bangladesh have had differences over sharing the waters of the ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ganga
Why: The Farakka issue concerns the sharing of the Ganga's waters.
Why not the others:
(A) The Indus is shared with Pakistan.
(C) and (D) flow only within India.
Key point: River waters are a key issue in India–Bangladesh relations.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why movements oppose large dams
questions.question: Why have many environmental movements in the South opposed the building of large dams?
options: A) Because dams always stop the flow of rivers completely
B) Because the UN has banned the building of large dams
C) Because dams uproot people and harm ecosystems
D) Because dams are built only by foreign governments
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because dams uproot people and harm ecosystems
Why: Large dams submerge land and forests and uproot local communities, which sparked protest movements.
Why not the others:
(A) Dams regulate flow; they do not stop it completely.
(B) No such ban exists.
(D) Most dams are built by national governments.
Key point: Anti-dam movements link environment and justice.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Not part of the consensus of the coalition era
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT part of the growing consensus among parties in the coalition era?
options: A) Rejection of the new economic policies
B) Acceptance of the claims of backward castes
C) Acceptance of the role of State-level parties
D) Emphasis on pragmatism over ideology
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Rejection of the new economic policies
Why: Most parties came to accept the new economic policies; they did not reject them.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are elements of the consensus NCERT describes.
Key point: Parties came to agree on several issues despite their rivalry.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: How long Vajpayee's first government lasted
questions.question: In 1996, the BJP government led by Atal Behari Vajpayee lasted only ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) thirteen days
Why: Vajpayee's first government lasted thirteen days, as it could not win a majority.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) give the wrong duration.
Key point: Without a majority, the 1996 government fell almost at once.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Venue of the first NAM summit
questions.question: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in 1961 at ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Belgrade
Why: The first NAM summit met in Belgrade in 1961.
Why not the others:
(B) Bandung hosted the Afro-Asian conference of 1955.
(C) New Delhi was not the venue.
(D) Havana was not the venue.
Key point: Belgrade 1961 marked the founding of NAM.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Leader of the Dravidian movement
questions.question: The Dravidian movement in Tamil Nadu was led by E.V. Ramasami, popularly known as ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Periyar
Why: E.V. Ramasami was called Periyar.
Why not the others:
(A) Anna was C.N. Annadurai.
(C) Kamaraj was a Congress leader.
(D) Netaji was Subhas Chandra Bose.
Key point: Periyar led the movement against Brahminical dominance and Hindi.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why the UN remains relevant
questions.question: Despite its flaws, why is the UN considered important for the world?
options: A) It can overrule the laws of every member state
B) It is a forum where states can talk and cooperate
C) It has an army that can defeat any country
D) It controls the budgets of its member countries
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It is a forum where states can talk and cooperate
Why: The UN brings states together to talk and cooperate, which no other body does on the same scale.
Why not the others:
(A) It cannot overrule national laws.
(C) It has no army of its own.
(D) It does not control national budgets.
Key point: The UN's value lies in being a global forum.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN agencies and their work
questions.question:
Match List-I (Agency) with List-II (Area of work).

List-I
(A) WHO
(B) UNHCR
(C) UNESCO
(D) ILO

List-II
(I) Rights of workers
(II) Education, science and culture
(III) Health
(IV) Refugees
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: The WHO works on health (III). The UNHCR protects refugees (IV). UNESCO covers education, science and culture (II). The ILO deals with workers' rights (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps the WHO and UNHCR. Option (C) swaps the UNHCR and UNESCO. Option (D) swaps UNESCO and the ILO.
Key point: Specialised agencies carry out much of the UN's work.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Why the US backed military rule in Pakistan
questions.question: Why did the US often support military rulers in Pakistan?
options: A) Because Pakistan was a permanent member of the UN Security Council
B) Because the US wanted to end democracy across all of Asia
C) Because Pakistan had asked the US to take over its army
D) Because it valued Pakistan as an ally, first in the Cold War
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because it valued Pakistan as an ally, first in the Cold War
Why: The US saw Pakistan as a useful ally, first against the Soviet Union and later against terrorism, and backed its rulers.
Why not the others:
(A) Pakistan is not a permanent member.
(B) The US had no such aim.
(C) No such request was made.
Key point: Outside support helped military regimes in Pakistan survive.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Model of economy India adopted
questions.question: By combining a large public sector with private enterprise, India adopted a ________ economy.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) mixed
Why: India chose a mixed economy, with both public and private sectors.
Why not the others:
(A) A laissez-faire economy leaves everything to the market.
(C) A command economy is wholly run by the state.
(D) A barter economy has no money.
Key point: India's model borrowed from both capitalism and socialism.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Why leaders first hesitated over linguistic States
questions.question: Why were national leaders at first reluctant to reorganise States on the basis of language?
options: A) Because no Indian language had a written script
B) Because the Constitution banned any change in State borders
C) Because the British had drawn borders that were perfect
D) Because they feared it could lead to division and disruption
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because they feared it could lead to division and disruption
Why: After Partition, leaders worried that linguistic States might encourage division and distract from other tasks.
Why not the others:
(A) Indian languages have rich written traditions.
(B) The Constitution allows Parliament to change borders.
(C) The colonial borders were administrative and arbitrary.
Key point: The fear of disintegration shaped early caution.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Religion and caste in politics, 1985–1992, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The foundation ceremony (shilanyas) is held at Ayodhya
(B) The government decides to implement the Mandal recommendations
(C) The Supreme Court decides the Shah Bano case
(D) The disputed structure at Ayodhya is demolished
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Why: (C) The Shah Bano judgement came in 1985. (A) The shilanyas took place in 1989. (B) The Mandal decision came in 1990. (D) The demolition took place in 1992.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the shilanyas before Shah Bano. Option (B) puts Mandal before the shilanyas. Option (C) puts the demolition before the Mandal decision.
Key point: 1985 → 1989 → 1990 → 1992.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Why the North-East felt cut off
questions.question: Why did the people of the North-East feel isolated from the rest of India?
options: A) Because of poor communication links and a narrow land connection
B) Because the region had no State governments until 1990
C) Because its people did not take part in national elections
D) Because Parliament had no members from the North-East
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Because of poor communication links and a narrow land connection
Why: The region is linked to the rest of India by a narrow strip and had weak communications, which deepened its sense of isolation.
Why not the others:
(B) Several States existed long before 1990.
(C) People there have always voted.
(D) The North-East is represented in Parliament.
Key point: Geography and neglect fed regional grievances.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Thinker who coined the term Hindutva
questions.question: The term 'Hindutva' was coined by ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) V.D. Savarkar
Why: V.D. Savarkar coined the term Hindutva.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were later leaders who drew on the idea.
Key point: Savarkar defined Hindutva as the basis of Indian nationhood.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: The Planning Commission — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 by a resolution of the Government of India.
(B) The Prime Minister was the chairperson of the Planning Commission.
(C) The Planning Commission was created by the Constitution itself.
(D) The First Five Year Plan began in 1951.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Planning Commission was not a constitutional body; it was set up by a simple government resolution.
Why not the others: (A) It was set up in March 1950. (B) The PM chaired it. (D) The First Plan began in 1951. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The Planning Commission was an advisory body, not a constitutional one.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Seat of the International Court of Justice
questions.question: The International Court of Justice is located at ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Hague
Why: The ICJ sits at The Hague in the Netherlands.
Why not the others:
(A) Geneva hosts several UN agencies.
(B) New York is the UN headquarters.
(C) Vienna hosts the IAEA.
Key point: The ICJ is the only principal organ not based in New York.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: How technology can strengthen states
questions.question: Why do some argue that globalisation can actually increase the power of states?
options: A) Because it abolishes all multinational companies
B) Because it bans the movement of capital
C) Because technology helps states watch their citizens
D) Because it ends all trade between countries
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because technology helps states watch their citizens
Why: Modern technology lets states collect information and rule more effectively.
Why not the others:
(A) MNCs have grown, not vanished.
(B) Capital moves more freely.
(D) Trade has expanded.
Key point: Globalisation does not always weaken the state.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: New States and the States they came from
questions.question:
Match List-I (State) with List-II (Carved out of).

List-I
(A) Haryana
(B) Gujarat
(C) Jharkhand
(D) Uttarakhand

List-II
(I) Uttar Pradesh
(II) Punjab
(III) Bombay State
(IV) Bihar
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Haryana was carved out of Punjab (II). Gujarat came out of Bombay State (III). Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar (IV). Uttarakhand was carved out of Uttar Pradesh (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Haryana and Gujarat. Option (C) swaps Gujarat and Jharkhand. Option (D) swaps Jharkhand and Uttarakhand.
Key point: The map of States has kept changing since 1956.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Why the EU carries political weight
questions.question: Why is the European Union seen as a political as well as an economic force?
options: A) It has a single army under one commander
B) Two members held permanent UNSC seats
C) It holds a special veto inside the WTO
D) All of its members also belong to ASEAN
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Two members held permanent UNSC seats
Why: Britain and France, then EU members, held permanent seats and vetoes in the Security Council, giving the EU political weight.
Why not the others:
(A) The EU has no single army.
(C) The WTO has no veto.
(D) EU members are not in ASEAN.
Key point: The EU's influence goes beyond trade.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: From revolution to collapse, 1917–1991, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Gorbachev becomes the leader of the Soviet Union
(B) The Berlin Wall falls
(C) Hardliners attempt a coup against Gorbachev
(D) The Bolshevik revolution takes place
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (A), (B), (C)
Why: (D) The revolution came in 1917. (A) Gorbachev took over in 1985. (B) The Berlin Wall fell in 1989. (C) The coup was attempted in August 1991.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts Gorbachev before the revolution. Option (C) puts the Berlin Wall before Gorbachev. Option (D) puts the coup before the Berlin Wall.
Key point: 1917 → 1985 → 1989 → 1991.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Not an example of a global commons
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a global commons?
options: C) The ocean floor beyond national limits
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Ganga river basin
Why: The Ganga basin lies within national territory. Global commons lie outside any one state's jurisdiction.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are global commons.
Key point: Global commons need international management.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Not a founding member of ASEAN
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the founding members of ASEAN?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Vietnam
Why: Vietnam joined ASEAN later, in 1995.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) founded ASEAN in 1967, with Malaysia and the Philippines.
Key point: ASEAN was founded by five states.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What carries ideas round the world fastest today
questions.question: Ideas now travel across the world faster than ever, mainly because of advances in ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) communication technology
Why: The internet and other communication technologies spread ideas almost instantly.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not account for today's speed.
Key point: Technology is a key cause of globalisation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Countries and facts from Asia and Europe
questions.question:
Match List-I (Country) with List-II (Fact).

List-I
(A) China
(B) Japan
(C) Britain
(D) Malaysia

List-II
(I) Kept out of the European market under Margaret Thatcher
(II) Privatised agriculture in 1982
(III) A founding member of ASEAN in 1967
(IV) Spends only about one per cent of its GDP on defence
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: China privatised agriculture in 1982 (II). Japan spends about one per cent of its GDP on defence (IV). Britain under Thatcher kept out of the European market (I). Malaysia was an ASEAN founder (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps China and Japan. Option (B) swaps Japan and Britain. Option (C) swaps Britain and Malaysia.
Key point: New centres of power differ in their strengths.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Phrases from the politics of 1967–1971
questions.question:
Match List-I (Phrase) with List-II (What it referred to).

List-I
(A) 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram'
(B) Grand Alliance
(C) 'Garibi hatao'
(D) 'Political earthquake'

List-II
(I) The coming together of non-communist opposition parties in 1971
(II) The results of the 1967 elections
(III) Frequent defections by legislators
(IV) Indira Gandhi's slogan in the 1971 election
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram' described frequent defections (III). The Grand Alliance brought the non-communist opposition together in 1971 (I). 'Garibi hatao' was Indira Gandhi's slogan in 1971 (IV). The 1967 results were called a political earthquake (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the first two phrases. Option (B) swaps the Grand Alliance and 'garibi hatao'. Option (D) swaps 'garibi hatao' and 'political earthquake'.
Key point: 1967–71 was a turbulent period of defections and realignment.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Kyoto and the Earth Summit — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) India and China were required to cut their emissions under the Kyoto Protocol.
(B) The Earth Summit produced Agenda 21.
(C) The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in 1997.
(D) India ratified the Kyoto Protocol in August 2002.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: India and China were exempt from the Kyoto targets.
Why not the others: (B) Agenda 21 came from Rio. (C) Kyoto was agreed in 1997. (D) India ratified it in 2002. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Kyoto's targets applied to industrialised countries.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Basis of post-Cold War India–Russia ties
questions.question: Why have India and Russia stayed close partners since 1991?
options: A) Because both are full members of NATO
B) Because they share one common currency
C) Because Russia is a member of SAARC
D) Because both favour a multipolar world
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because both favour a multipolar world
Why: Both countries share a vision of a multipolar world in which power is spread among many states.
Why not the others:
(A) Neither is a NATO member.
(B) They have separate currencies.
(C) Russia is not in SAARC.
Key point: A multipolar vision underpins India–Russia ties.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Why the Congress started with an edge in early elections
questions.question: Why did the Congress enjoy a great advantage in the first general elections?
options: A) Because it was the only party allowed to field candidates
B) Because the British had handed it control of the army
C) Because it had inherited the legacy of the national movement
D) Because it had promised to restore the princely states
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because it had inherited the legacy of the national movement
Why: The Congress had led the freedom struggle and had an organisation across the country, which gave it a head start.
Why not the others:
(A) Many parties contested.
(B) No such thing happened.
(D) It had integrated the princely states.
Key point: The legacy of the freedom movement underpinned Congress dominance.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: A lesson of the Emergency
questions.question: Which of the following is drawn as a lesson from the Emergency?
options: A) Democracy in India can never be suspended in any form at all
B) Emergency powers should be given to the courts alone
C) Elections should be held only once every ten years
D) Rights can be taken away easily, so citizens must be vigilant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Rights can be taken away easily, so citizens must be vigilant
Why: The Emergency showed how quickly rights could be taken away and how valuable they are.
Why not the others:
(A) The Emergency showed that it could be suspended.
(B) That was not a lesson drawn.
(C) No one drew that conclusion.
Key point: The Emergency strengthened awareness of civil liberties.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Where the Navnirman movement began
questions.question: The students' movement of 1974 known as the Navnirman Andolan began in ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Gujarat
Why: The Navnirman movement was a student agitation in Gujarat in 1974.
Why not the others:
(A) Bihar had the separate JP-led movement.
(B) and (D) did not see this movement.
Key point: Gujarat and Bihar movements set the stage for the Emergency.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: The first elections and Congress dominance — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner of India.
(B) The CPI emerged as the second largest party in the Lok Sabha in 1952.
(C) In 1957, a CPI-led government came to power in Kerala.
(D) The Congress won fewer than half of the Lok Sabha seats in 1952.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: the Congress won 364 of the 489 seats in 1952.
Why not the others: Option (A) leaves out the true statement (C). Options (B) and (C) include the false statement (D).
Key point: The Congress won a sweeping majority in the first election.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Democracy in South Asia's smaller states — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Nepal became a democratic republic after the monarchy was abolished in 2008.
(B) Bhutan held its first parliamentary elections in 2008.
(C) The Maldives became a republic in 1968.
(D) The Indian Peace Keeping Force stayed in Sri Lanka until 2001.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. (D) is wrong: the IPKF withdrew in 1989.
Why not the others: Option (A) leaves out the true statement (C). Options (B) and (D) include the false statement (D).
Key point: Democracy has spread unevenly across South Asia.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Region with most HIV-AIDS cases in 2003
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For most of modern history, security meant protecting a state against military attack from outside. Thinking on security has since widened. The idea of human security places people, rather than territories or governments, at the centre. Some scholars would limit it to violent threats against individuals. Others would add hunger, disease and natural disasters, which kill far more people than wars do. The broadest version speaks of 'freedom from want' and 'freedom from fear'. New sources of insecurity have also drawn attention. Global poverty is one: the gap between rich and poor countries leaves millions exposed to risks they cannot control. Health epidemics are another. By 2003, about 4 crore people across the world were infected with HIV-AIDS, two-thirds of them in Africa. Diseases of this kind do not stop at national frontiers, and no single government can contain them on its own. For this reason, dealing with such threats calls for cooperation. Cooperative security may involve international organisations such as the UN and the WHO, non-governmental organisations, business corporations and even eminent persons. It may be bilateral, regional, continental or global, depending on the nature of the threat.

Question: According to the passage, where were about two-thirds of the people infected with HIV-AIDS in 2003?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) In Africa
Why: The passage says that of about 4 crore people infected by 2003, two-thirds were in Africa.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not named in the passage.
Key point: The burden of HIV-AIDS fell most heavily on Africa.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Broadest version of human security
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Which formulation does the passage describe as the broadest version of human security?
options: A) Protection of borders against armed attack
B) Protection of individuals from violent threats only
C) Protection of governments from their own citizens
D) Freedom from want and freedom from fear
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Freedom from want and freedom from fear
Why: The passage says the broadest version speaks of 'freedom from want' and 'freedom from fear'.
Why not the others:
(A) That is the traditional idea of security.
(B) That is the narrowest version of human security.
(C) The passage does not mention this.
Key point: Human security can be defined more or less widely.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Why epidemics are treated as a security issue

Question: Why, according to the passage, do epidemics like HIV-AIDS call for cooperation?
options: A) They spread across frontiers beyond any one state's control.
B) They affect only the poorest people within the richest countries.
C) They are caused by wars between neighbouring states.
D) They can be ended quickly by military action.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) They spread across frontiers beyond any one state's control.
Why: The passage says such diseases do not stop at frontiers and no single government can contain them on its own.
Why not the others:
(B) The passage points to poor countries, especially in Africa.
(C) The passage does not link epidemics to wars.
(D) The passage does not suggest military action.
Key point: Threats that cross borders need joint responses.

Question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a possible participant in cooperative security?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A great-power military alliance
Why: The passage lists international organisations, NGOs, business corporations and eminent persons. It does not mention a military alliance.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are named in the passage.
Key point: Cooperative security involves many kinds of actors, not just states.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: How the newer view changes the idea of security
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For most of modern history, security meant protecting a state against military attack from outside. Thinking on security has since widened. The idea of human security places people, rather than territories or governments, at the centre. Some scholars would limit it to violent threats against individuals. It may be bilateral, regional, continental or global, depending on the nature of the threat.

Question: What does the passage suggest about the newer thinking on security, compared with the traditional view?
options: A) It holds that states no longer face any external threats.
B) It widens both what counts as a threat and who must respond.
C) It treats disease and poverty as purely private matters.
D) It leaves security to governments acting entirely on their own.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It widens both what counts as a threat and who must respond.
Why: The passage adds hunger, disease and poverty to the list of threats and names many actors beyond states who must cooperate.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage does not deny external threats.
(C) The passage treats them as security threats.
(D) The passage stresses cooperation.
Key point: The scope of security has broadened in both threats and actors.
